To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

matches.title: Idea2Prior: Auditable Paper Retrieval and Ranking from Research Ideas
matches.abstract_excerpt: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present IDEA2PRIOR, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

The hard switch is the simplest implementation of the shape-then-release principle. The early intervention is used to steer the optimization trajectory away from spectrally concentrated regimes, rather than to prescribe a persistent spectral constraint. Once released, the spectrum is free to adapt to the task objective. Empirically, we find that part of the higher-effective-rank state induced during the active stage persists after release, allowing the optimization benefit to continue without maintaining the orthogonal regularizer. Unless otherwise specified, we use τ = 0.25 \tau=0.25 throughout the paper; Section 5 studies sensitivity to the release point. Beyond soft orthogonality. Soft orthogonality defines the default ORCA optimizer, but the underlying shape-then-release principle is not tied to this particular spectral operator. In Section 5, we replace soft orthogonal shaping with alternative early spectral interventions, including Pion-start and DiagSVD variants. These methods differ in how the spectral state is shaped during the active stage; once the active window ends, the intervention is removed and all variants continue with the same released Muon dynamics. This provides a controlled way to study whether the benefit of early spectral intervention extends beyond soft orthogonality itself.

Implementation and overhead. In the standard setting, ORCA adds two matrix multiplications per weight matrix during shaping without changing the communication complexity; the remaining operations are fused into the optimizer update. Our Muon baseline performs 24 matrix multiplications across eight Newton–Schulz iterations, so shaping increases the multiplication count by 2 / 24 = 8.3 % 2/24=8.3\% . This extra work disappears after release. We batch matrices of identical shapes to reduce kernel launches, use dedicated kernels, and form the Gram matrix along the shorter dimension. On the 8B MoE model, average distributed optimizer update time is 227.2 ​ ms 227.2\,\mathrm{ms} for Muon and 237.4 ​ ms 237.4\,\mathrm{ms} for ORCA. The 10.2 ​ ms 10.2\,\mathrm{ms} difference amounts to approximately 0.8 % 0.8\% of a roughly 1.3 ​ s 1.3\,\mathrm{s} training step. Peak memory is 101.41 ​ GB 101.41\,\mathrm{GB} and 101.66 ​ GB 101.66\,\mathrm{GB} , respectively. Overall, ORCA incurs negligible additional training overhead in this configuration.

ORCA uses temporary early orthogonality regularization to accelerate LLM training, achieving lower validation loss. Its central insight is that optimizers can both choose better update directions and steer early training toward regions where loss is easier to reduce. We hope this perspective inspires future optimizer design.

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

Validation loss was monitored throughout and remained almost exactly at training loss, so overfitting is not a concern. Every Muon variant drops the loss faster than AdamW over the first hundred steps (Figure 3 (b)), and the lead grows with how much of the spectrum is lifted. Lifting only the top few directions with a high τ \tau already gets much of Muon’s early advantage, but the lead reverses within a few hundred steps, and every top dose ends up behind AdamW with warmup, the smallest ones even behind NSGD (Table 1 ). This is not a matter of step size. Raising the learning rate of the top variants only makes them worse and collapses their rank further (Figure 5 (c)), while Muon at a tenth of its learning rate loses just 0.05. Figure 3 (c,d) plots the final loss against τ \tau and against the fraction of the momentum that is orthogonalized. For both top and bottom targeting, loss falls monotonically with the portion of directions orthogonalized. However, the two arms are not symmetric. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix gets within 0.03 of Muon while orthogonalizing only about 13% of the momentum matrix’s magnitude, while lifting only the top directions remains well short even when they make up 96% of it, and the smallest top doses do worse than lifting nothing. This answers one part of our original question. Despite being a very small portion of the momentum magnitude, the small singular values are not noise. The model can be usefully trained on them, but only once they are amplified to full scale. Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

Code: https://github.com/brain-lab-research/monarch-muon Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch–Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch–Muon improves over Monarch–AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch–Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

The parameterization itself offers another route to efficiency. Reducing the number of trainable parameters reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer buffers together. For Muon, a suitable structure can also replace large orthogonalization problems with smaller ones. The important question is whether this computationally cheaper representation retains the optimization benefit of matrix-aware updates. Figure 1 : Training-step breakdown and optimizer-state memory for the 6.89B dense reference at microbatch 4 and four accumulation steps, from the same runs as Table 2 . Bars show median phase timings; labels give median full-step wall time. Periodic projection refreshes are excluded. Monarch–Muon uses four blocks and reduces both optimizer-state memory and optimizer-step overhead. We introduce Monarch–Muon, which parameterizes selected weights with Monarch factors ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and applies Muon directly to their trainable blocks. This representation uses fewer parameters while retaining the ability to express full-rank transformations, reducing storage for weights, gradients, and optimizer state. The smaller blocks also make Muon’s orthogonalization cheaper. In dense and mixture-of-experts pretraining, Muon improves validation loss over AdamW at fixed Monarch structure. Systems measurements show that the computational savings grow with matrix size, making the approach particularly effective at larger scales.

Structure reduces more than the optimizer state: it also compresses the trainable weights and gradients. For Muon, the smaller blocks additionally reduce the cost of orthogonalization. The benefit grows with width because cheaper orthogonalization is increasingly accompanied by cheaper forward and backward passes. At this scale, Monarch–Muon also has the shortest full step and lowest peak memory among the measured state-efficient methods, even though their optimizer steps alone are cheaper. passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

Effective capacity and optimization geometry. That LoRA’s update carries a stable rank well below its nominal rank is likewise established, as a pathology to engineer away ( Lion et al., 2025 ) and as a sweep locating where validation accuracy turns ( Awofeso et al., 2025 ) ; we add its placement relative to interpolation and an intervention on it. Parameterization matters beyond expressivity ( Shuttleworth et al., 2025 ) , and learning rate interacts with rank through initialization and scaling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , which is why the shared-rate sweep is checked against per-arm rates (each at its own rate) on every backbone (Section 5.3 , Appendices C.2 and C.3 ). The optimization geometry of the factored parameterization is mapped: freezing one factor ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) or both ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) , preconditioning the gradient ( Zhang & Pilanci, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2026 ) , and showing that different factorizations of one Δ ​ W \Delta W converge differently ( Castin et al., 2026 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) . Those results concern training and generalization of the factorization; ours concern where the post-peak branch reaches dense risk (Section 5.3 ). Chang et al. (2025) use “double descent” for a transient training-loss divergence, a different object. Memorization and calibration under noise. Interpolating noisy labels forces memorization ( Zhang et al., 2017 ; Feldman & Zhang, 2020 ) , and calibration itself depends on overparameterization in high-dimensional models ( Clarté et al., 2023 ) , which is why we separate the risk we measure from the temperature it is read at (Section 5.6 ).

The rise is not (mostly) miscalibration. Fitting a temperature on a held-out clean split never used for training ( Guo et al., 2017 ) leaves 83 % 83\% of the noisy cliff standing ( 0.44 0.44 vs. 0.53 0.53 nats, 5 5 seeds), rescaling leaves the accuracy drop unchanged, and expected calibration error, Brier score and selective-risk area all degrade across the same range ( Naeini et al., 2015 ; Brier, 1950 ; Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017 ; Geifman et al., 2019 ) . With clean labels calibration removes about half the rise instead (Table 12 ). Under label noise, the cliff is mostly real error rather than overconfidence. Noise and augmentation change only the cliff’s depth. CIFAR-100N human re-annotation labels ( Wei et al., 2022 ) replicate the cliff with larger amplitude. Sweeping η ∈ { 10 , 20 , 40 , 60 } % \eta\in\{10,20,40,60\}\% keeps the valley pinned at r = 1 r{=}1 while the amplitude grows monotonically, and augmentation shrinks the amplitude without changing the shape or adding a second descent (Appendix E.1 ). The peak moves with the training budget. From 40 40 to 80 80 epochs it shifts from r = 64 r{=}64 to r = 32 r{=}32 , and at 20 20 epochs risk is monotone in rank because low ranks have not yet interpolated. The peak reflects interpolation status at the current budget ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) , so the protocol locates r interp r_{\mathrm{interp}} per budget. Neither longer training nor α / r \alpha/r scaling returns the tail to the valley (Appendix B.1 ).

Model selection shrinks the cliff without removing it. Selecting learning rate, weight decay and stopping epoch on a clean validation split reduces the cliff from 0.53 0.53 to 0.16 0.16 nats. The selected models retain the rank ordering on fresh seeds, and every selected checkpoint precedes interpolation (Appendix E.2 ), which is the mechanism: selection escapes the cliff by declining to interpolate, not by crossing it. Because per-rank selection includes no dense arm, it bears on the shape of the axis and not on the gap to dense. No tested setting removes the cliff once ranks interpolate. Corrupting the frozen backbone only deepens the cliff, and its shape persists through changes in data size, learning rate, weight decay, scaling, adapter placement and dataset (Appendices C.2 , E.1 and E.3 ; Table 15 ). Architecture decides too. A ResNet completes the descent on these subsets; a width-scaled ViT trained from scratch does not (Appendix B.2 ), recovering 0.56 0.56 of 3.23 3.23 nats, the final-ascent regime of Xue et al. (2024) . Dense-block fine-tuning of a transformer reaches Rec = 0.82 \mathrm{Rec}{=}0.82 , so the rank axis’s shallow far side is not a transformer property. Scope. The experiments cover noisy image and text classification with AdamW, synthetic and human label noise, and budgets up to 160 160 epochs. The dense reference is module-matched, training the projections LoRA adapts rather than the whole network; the dense-block axis of Section 5.5 unfreezes up to six full blocks. Test NLL is the primary measurement, and accuracy follows its ordering inside the parameter-saving window but can diverge at larger ranks. Where LoRA crosses dense depends on the protocol and the grid.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

passages.text: Under the shared learning rate, every post-peak rank that still saves parameters trails module-matched dense fine-tuning on the three vision backbones with a cliff (Appendix C.1 ) and on a 7 7 B language model (Appendix C.3 ). Per-arm learning rates narrow this gap without closing it (Appendix C.2 ), and Appendix C.4 explains why the tail is graded against dense rather than against the pre-peak valley.

passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

BrowseComp-Plus CM requires searching 553 million ClimbMix documents, our largest corpus. CORE again leads in both accuracy and recall for every agent. Its advantage is most pronounced with Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B. CORE outperforms OpenResearcher by 14.03 points. With GPT-5.4, CORE raises accuracy to 68.42%, compared with 56.14% for OpenResearcher and 50.88% for Tongyi DeepResearch. With Qwen3.8-27B, Tongyi DeepResearch is the stronger baseline in accuracy, and CORE still exceeds both baselines in accuracy and recall.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

decision.reason: The ten selections cover the profile’s central questions: training for low-rank compressibility, spectral optimization, LoRA rank and generalization, memory-efficient pretraining, and research-agent harnesses.
